newsitem.title: USA: S&P affirms Atrium Companies Inc ratings.
newsitem.headline: S&P affirms Atrium Companies Inc ratings.

text.p: Standard & Poor's today has affirmed the double-'B'-minus corporate credit rating and single-'B' subordinated debt rating of Atrium Companies Inc.
The ratings have been removed from CreditWatch, where they were placed with negative implications June 25, 1997 following Atrium's announced plan to acquire Ply Gem Industries Inc.
Ply Gem instead has accepted a higher bid from single-'B'-plus rated Nortek Inc. and will reportedly pay Atrium break-up fees and expenses totaling about $12 million.
The ratings outlook on Atrium is stable.

The ratings reflect Atrium's leading position in the cyclical U.S. window and door market, satisfactory operating margins, and rising income, but also a modest sales base, low earnings and cash flow protection measures, and aggressive use of debt.
Atrium is one of the two largest aluminum window manufacturers in its primary market (Southwest, South, and Southeast U.S.), which includes some of the fastest-growing residential housing areas.
Atrium's fundamentals are enhanced by well known brand names, distribution strengths, and cost benefits from vertically integrated operations.

Although business is quite cyclical, as roughly 70% of revenues are derived from new home construction, cyclicality should be tempered by acquisitions and other steps to grow sales to the remodel/replacement sector and to diversify the geographic focus.
Income is expected to remain in an uptrend for the next couple of years, aided by favorable levels of construction activity, especially in Atrium's primary market.
Operating margins are satisfactory at 14%, despite meaningful losses in wood windows. Capital spending needs are modest, thus bolstering free cash flows.

There is flexibility in the capital structure for debt to be increased modestly without harming credit quality. Cash interest coverage (after capital outlays) over the next few years is expected to be 2.0 times (x)-2.5x, and funds from operations to debt is anticipated to average about 15%.
Standard & Poor's anticipates that internal cash generation should be able to fund periodic moderate-sized acquisitions, while sustaining a financial profile appropriate for the rating.
Upside prospects are tempered by the potential for a slowdown in the company's markets and by modest cash flows that make credit quality ratios vulnerable to wide swings.
